title: Is No-Cost EMI Really Free? The Hidden Costs Indians Miss
summary: No-cost EMI always has a cost; the question is who pays it. Here's what to check before every festive sale purchase.
content:
No-cost EMI is rarely free. The interest on your purchase is always being paid by someone, and that someone is usually either the merchant, a cash discount you didn't get, or a markup baked into the price. Before any festive sale purchase, knowing which version you're looking at takes about 60 seconds and can save you Rs 2,000 or more.

Key Takeaways

  • No-cost EMI shifts the interest cost; it doesn't eliminate it. The merchant usually pays your bank directly through a model called subvention.
  • The most common hidden cost isn't a fee. It's the upfront cash discount you lose by choosing EMI over an outright purchase.
  • Processing fees of Rs 199 to Rs 499 apply on most no-cost EMI transactions, plus 18% GST.
  • One missed payment often triggers retroactive interest on the full original amount, wiping out the savings.
  • During Diwali sales, the no-cost EMI price on many products is Rs 1,000 to Rs 5,000 higher than the cash price.

How does no-cost EMI actually work?

No-cost EMI works through merchant subvention. The seller pays your bank the interest amount upfront, so your instalments cover only the principal. A Rs 30,000 phone on a 3-month plan costs Rs 10,000 per month, and the brand quietly covers the bank's 2% monthly interest. You pay no interest because the seller did.

That's the most straightforward version. The second model is less obvious: some sellers offer a cash discount, say Rs 3,000 off for immediate payment, but don't apply it if you choose EMI. You never pay interest in name, but you paid Rs 3,000 more than you needed to. Functionally identical.

A third version exists on some platforms: the price under no-cost EMI is simply higher than the cash price. Same product, seperate prices depending on payment method. Less common on Flipkart and Amazon but worth checking during sales.

What does no-cost EMI actually cost you?

Even in a genuine no-cost EMI deal, three real costs still apply: a processing fee of Rs 199 to Rs 499 plus 18% GST, higher credit card utilization that can lower your CIBIL score, and the risk of retroactive interest if you miss even one payment. The first is small. The second and third aren't.

Processing fees. Most banks charge between Rs 199 and Rs 499 per transaction. HDFC Bank charges Rs 299, SBI charges Rs 269, ICICI and Axis Bank around Rs 199, as of the most recent publicly available terms. GST at 18% adds Rs 36 to Rs 90 on top. On a Rs 10,000 purchase, that's 3 to 5 percent on the first instalment alone.

Credit utilization. When you take a no-cost EMI on a credit card, the full purchase amount is typically blocked against your limit on day one. A Rs 50,000 laptop on a 6-month EMI blocks Rs 50,000 on the first day, not Rs 8,333. If your total credit limit is Rs 1,00,000, you've used 50% of it. Credit scores start taking a hit once utilization crosses 30%.

The missed-payment trap. Most bank EMI agreements include this clause: miss one payment, and the interest waiver is cancelled retroactively. The bank recalculates interest from the start at the standard rate, usually 1.5 to 3% per month, and adds the total to your next statement. One missed payment on a Rs 60,000 purchase over 6 months can generate a surprise charge of Rs 5,000 to Rs 8,000.

No-cost EMI vs. outright purchase: when each makes sense

FactorNo-Cost EMIOutright Purchase
Immediate cash impactLow (monthly payments)High (single payment)
Total costSlightly higher due to processing fee and GSTUsually lower if cash discount applies
CIBIL score impactRaises credit utilization initiallyNo impact
Default riskRetroactive interest if payment is missedNone
Best forLarge planned purchases when cash is tightWhen cash discount exists or amount is small

A reasonable rule of thumb: if the total extra you would pay on EMI (processing fee plus forgone discount) is under Rs 500, EMI is worth the cash flow convenience on a large purchase. Above Rs 1,000, pay upfront.

What to check before placing a no-cost EMI order

  1. Look for a cash discount. Many product pages show a separate additional discount for non-EMI payment. Subtract that from the EMI price. The difference is your real cost of choosing EMI.
  2. Find the processing fee. Scroll to the payment step or tap the i icon next to the no-cost EMI option. Banks are required to display this before you confirm the order.
  3. Calculate the total outflow. Monthly instalment times number of months, plus processing fee and GST. Compare this to the best cash price available, including any bank-card discount.
  4. Check your reason for using EMI. No-cost EMI makes sense when you have the cash but want to preserve your savings or emergency fund. It doesn't make sense if you're choosing it becuase you couldn't otherwise afford the product. That's how EMIs quietly become a debt pattern.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does no-cost EMI affect your CIBIL score?

Yes, in two ways. The full purchase amount is blocked on your credit limit from day one, raising your credit utilization ratio. Utilization above 30% can lower your score. And if you miss a payment, the bank reports it as a default, which hurts your score far more significantly than high utilization alone does.

Is no-cost EMI available on debit cards in India?

Yes, but it works differently. Debit card no-cost EMI deducts a fixed amount from your account each month. There's no credit utilization impact, but your account needs sufficient balance every month. Processing fees still apply. HDFC, SBI, and Axis Bank are among the major banks offering this, though not all debit cards qualify.

Can you foreclose a no-cost EMI early?

Usually yes, but often with a foreclosure fee. The fee varies by bank, typically Rs 500 or 3% of the outstanding amount, whichever is higher. Some banks allow free foreclosure after a minimum number of instalments. Check your loan agreement before prepaying; in some cases the fee exceeds what you would save in remaining instalments.

Is no-cost EMI a good idea for large appliances?

Often yes, during genuine festive sales when prices are actually lower than usual. Compare the no-cost EMI price against two or three offline stores and other sites. If the sale discount is real and the processing fee is small relative to the purchase amount, a large appliance on no-cost EMI is one of the more sensible uses of the product.

What does subvention mean on a no-cost EMI?

Subvention is the payment the brand or merchant makes to your bank to cover your interest. You don't see this payment; it happens between the seller and the bank. Merchants often price products slightly higher on EMI-heavy platforms to recover this subvention cost, which is part of why the EMI price and cash price sometimes differ.

The short version

No-cost EMI shifts the interest cost to the merchant, or replaces it with a discount you don't get. The total you pay is usually slightly higher than the cash price once you factor in the processing fee, GST, and any forgone discount. For large planned purchases during genuine festive sales, EMI is often still a good deal. For anything you couldn't otherwise afford, it isn't.

Before clicking Place Order, spend 60 seconds comparing the EMI price to the best cash price and checking the processing fee. That one check is worth more than any EMI calculator app.

This post describes how no-cost EMI works and what to watch for. It's for information only, not financial advice. Always verify fees and terms with your bank before any purchase.
